The Cross-Process Realtime Gap

The one Week 5 channel that's registered for ticket.sla_breached but never actually fires — and why that's a real limit of this design, not a bug to fix here.

// Figure 6.10: realtime push (src/events/listeners/notifyRealtime.listener.js)
domainEvents.on(EVENTS.TICKET_SLA_BREACHED, (ticket) => {
  try {
    const io = getIO();
    if (!io) return;

    if (ticket.assignedAgentId) {
      io.to(`user:${ticket.assignedAgentId}`).emit(EVENTS.TICKET_SLA_BREACHED, ticket);
    } else {
      io.to('role:agent').emit(EVENTS.TICKET_SLA_BREACHED, ticket);
    }
  } catch (err) { /* ... */ }
});

This is registered for symmetry with the other two channels, but it's the one that never actually reaches a browser. Recall getIO() from Week 5: it returns undefined whenever initSocket() was never called in this process — built so a test importing app.js directly via supertest gets "no realtime channel available" instead of a crash. escalateOverdueTickets only ever emits ticket.sla_breached from inside the worker process (src/worker.js) — a process that never calls initSocket(), because it never creates an HTTP server at all. So getIO() here returns undefined, this handler returns immediately, and the push never happens.

The in-app and email channels don't have this problem, and the reason why is worth naming precisely: Prisma and nodemailer both talk to infrastructure that's genuinely shared across processes — the same MySQL database, the same Mailpit SMTP server — so it doesn't matter which process writes the Notification row or sends the email. Socket.IO is different: the actual open TCP connections to connected browsers live only in the memory of whichever process called initSocket() — here, the API process. A second process has no way to reach into the first one's connection list.

This is a genuine limitation of the design as built in this course, not something to patch around here. A production system would reach for Socket.IO's Redis adapter (@socket.io/redis-adapter), which lets any process publish an event that every process's connected sockets can receive — out of scope for this module, but worth knowing this gap is why it exists, rather than assuming realtime notifications "just work" once a second process enters the picture.
